system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2123-05-31 18:58:00 to 2123-06-01 15:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted with severe left-sided lumbar back pain radiating to the thigh. MRI revealed lumbosacral spondylosis at L4-L5 with nerve root impingement but no malignancy or infection. He also had elevated alkaline phosphatase, prompting further evaluation. Abdominal MRI and liver biopsy showed bile duct changes suggestive of obstruction, and ERCP confirmed a benign stricture at the bile duct anastomosis. A stent was placed to relieve the obstruction, with plans for removal in three months. He developed transient urinary retention due to narcotics, managed with tamsulosin. Hepatitis C viral load was detected (genotype 1a), and outpatient treatment was arranged. He improved with pain management and was discharged home with stable transplant function, instructions for follow-up, and a plan for HCV therapy and stent removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel, one of the transplant surgery team. I see you came in after your ERCP today and are having some abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. After the procedure, I started feeling this pain in the middle and right side of my belly. It was pretty sharp at first, but it’s gotten a bit better since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Were you having nausea or vomiting? Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No nausea or vomiting. No fever either. I feel okay otherwise—just the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re passing gas, which is a positive sign. The team decided to admit you for observation because of the pain, even though you were supposed to go home. We want to make sure nothing serious develops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Was the procedure successful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The original stent was removed, and we found the same 5 mm stricture at the bile duct connection—no change from before. We placed two new stents to keep the duct open and help prevent future blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the narrowing is still there? Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s benign, meaning it’s not cancerous. It’s common after transplant. The stents will help keep the flow of bile normal. We’ll monitor it and likely remove the stents in a few months if things look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried it might be something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re also watching your labs. Your liver enzymes are a bit elevated, which we expected, and your lipase was normal—so no sign of pancreatitis. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, doctor. It’s much better—just a little sore when I press on it. I ate breakfast and felt fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your repeat labs look stable. The abdominal tenderness has improved, and you’re tolerating food well. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Is there anything I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call the transplant clinic if you develop fever, worsening pain, nausea, vomiting, or yellowing of the skin. Also, keep taking your tacrolimus and other meds as prescribed. We’ve added a short course of ciprofloxacin to prevent infection after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team will contact you for lab work and a clinic visit. Don’t take your tacrolimus until after your blood draw on lab days. Bring the dose with you so you can take it right after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to do that. Thanks, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours once the paperwork is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your discharge orders are in. You can go home soon. Here’s your updated medication list and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow everything closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—stay hydrated, eat small meals, and avoid sun exposure. Your skin is more sensitive now. Use sunscreen and wear a hat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I’ve been through this before, so I know the drill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember—no new meds without checking with the transplant team. Some drugs can interfere with your anti-rejection meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I won’t change anything without calling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor. I appreciate it.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted for observation following a scheduled ERCP during which the initial biliary stent was removed and two new stents were placed due to a persistent 5 mm benign stricture at the biliary anastomosis. He developed mild right and mid-abdominal pain post-procedure, prompting admission to the transplant surgery service. His pain improved overnight, he remained afebrile, passed flatus, and tolerated a regular diet. Labs showed stable liver function and no signs of pancreatitis. He was discharged home with instructions to continue immunosuppressive and supportive medications, a short course of ciprofloxacin, and close follow-up with the transplant clinic for monitoring and future stent management.
